title: What animal rights advocates get wrong
subtitle: Animal rights doesn't need anti-speciesism
author: Sophie Grace Chappell
introduction: Perhaps the most common defence of animal rights is based on the claim that it is wrong to discriminate on the grounds of species. Just as it is wrong to treat people differently on the basis of race or sex—so animal rights advocates argue—it is wrong to treat other animals differently on the basis of their species membership. In this article, Sophie Grace Chappell argues against this dominant view in animal ethics. Chappell argues for the inherent value of animals, not based on detached reasoning about discrimination, but instead based on an ethics of love and attention.
body:
How should we think about the (other) animals? I believe we should think about them as inherently valuable and deserving of protection—in short, as having rights. In that broad sense, this essay is a defence of animal rights.

At first glance, it might not look like that. In philosophy we don’t just want the right conclusions; we want the right conclusions for the right reasons. And a lot of the commonest arguments for animal rights don’t, in my view, give us the right reasons. So I start by unpicking some bad arguments for animal rights. Then I present what I hope is a better argument.

SUGGESTED VIEWING Humanity and the gods of nature With Slavoj Žižek, Jack Symes, Peter Singer, Nancy Sherman

Perhaps the commonest argument you hear for animal rights is built on this claim:

Anti-Speciesism: It is morally wrong to discriminate on the grounds of species.

Often Anti-Speciesism is argued for by analogy with two other positions allegedly parallel to it:

Anti-Racism: It is morally wrong to discriminate on the grounds of race.

Anti-Sexism: It is morally wrong to discriminate on the grounds of sex.

Are these positions analogous? Well, they do have this in common: all three are guaranteed trivially true by their wording. These three statements all say that it is morally wrong to “discriminate”. But as the word is usually defined, “discriminate” means “treat differently in a morally wrong way”. And it is not news that it is morally wrong to act in a morally wrong way. All three positions alike are trivial and uninformative.

So we need to replace “discriminate” with “treat beings differently”:

Anti-Speciesism 2: It is morally wrong to treat beings differently on the grounds of species.

Anti-Racism 2: It is morally wrong to treat beings differently on the grounds of race.

Anti-Sexism 2: It is morally wrong to treat beings differently on the grounds of sex.

The trouble with these positions is that they’re all false. To take them in reverse order:

Doctors regularly treat their female patients differently from their male ones: male patients don’t routinely get offered mammograms, and female patients don’t routinely get offered prostate checks.

Doctors sometimes treat patients of different races differently too, because there are some diseases to which some races are particularly genetically susceptible.

Doctors are professionally concerned with humans, not with animals of other species. And vets, who are professionally concerned with animals of other species, not with humans, treat different species of non-human animal very differently.

Distinctions of treatment between species are as commonplace as distinctions of treatment between races and sexes. None of them is automatically morally wrong.

It isn’t just medical professionals who make these distinctions between races, sexes, and species. You do too, if you make a special effort to make someone welcome at a party because she’s the only black person there; or if, as a philosophy tutor, you try to get the women in your discussion group to speak up because the men are monopolising the conversation; or if you take your dog for a walk, not your cat. Distinctions of treatment between species are as commonplace as distinctions of treatment between races and sexes. None of them is automatically morally wrong.

So what are people getting at when they protest against racism, sexism, and speciesism as morally wrong, and morally wrong in an analogous way? Maybe the real point is a more restricted one. Consider Shylock’s monologue from Shakespeare’s The Merchant of Venice.

Hath not a Jew eyes? Hath not a Jew hands, organs, dimensions, senses, affections, passions? Fed with the same food, hurt with the same weapons, subject to the same diseases, healed by the same means, warmed and cooled by the same winter and summer as a Christian is? If you prick us, do we not bleed? If you tickle us, do we not laugh? If you poison us, do we not die?

Shylock’s point is that pain in Jewish people is just as bad as pain in Christian people. This is something that anti-Semites do characteristically deny, as do other racists about other ethnic groups.

Alternatively, racists say that black people don’t even feel pain as white people do, or that “lower races” are not grieved by losing their children as “higher races” are. [1] This latter kind of claim is, of course, factually incorrect, and apparently motivated by a denial mechanism that is itself racist.

SUGGESTED VIEWING Martha Nussbaum: A new theory of ethics With Martha Nussbaum

Suppose that we can get people at least to agree on the facts about pain, as expressed by Shylock’s point. Then maybe the principle that we need is the following: “The same pain, in any being capable of feeling it, is equally bad.”

Applied to race and sex, this principle implies that it is wrong to say that the same pain matters less in a woman than in a man, or in a black person than a white one. Applied to species, it implies that it is wrong to deny that animals’ pain matters as much as human pain.

Is this principle true? I think so—at least roughly. There are slight complications, however, once we consider degrees of desert. Suppose Jane breaks her toe falling downstairs, while you break your toe trying to kick my cat Macavity.

Your broken-toe pain and Jane’s broken-toe pain are, let’s stipulate, the same pain. So if the equality principle were unrestrictedly true, your pain and Jane’s would be equally bad. But you, after all, are the bastard who tried to kick Macavity. So it would be very understandable for someone (e.g., me, as Macavity’s owner) to judge Jane’s broken-toe pain to be a worse state of affairs than yours. Indeed I might even say not only that the two pains aren’t equally bad, but that while Jane’s pain is bad, your pain is actually good—because you deserve it.

SUGGESTED VIEWING Humans and other animals With Kay Peggs, Jamie Blackett, Raymond Tallis, Melanie Challenger

Philosophers disagree about desert: some believe in it (e.g., me), some don’t. If we believe in desert, and if this case shows what I think it shows, then it is a counter-example to the unrestricted version of the equality principle. However, we can easily reformulate the principle to accommodate it: “Where there is no difference in desert, the same pain, in any being capable of feeling it, is equally bad.”

The amended principletells us that if we want to say that pain is less bad or more bad in one sex than the other, or one race than the others, or one species than the others, then we need to provide a factual basis for a difference in desert between sexes, races, or species.

People have sometimes tried to do this. People used to argue, citing Genesis 3.14-16, that snakes deserve to be destroyed, and that women deserve the pain of childbirth. People have all too often argued that various races, including primal peoples all over the world, deserve to be wiped out or enslaved or dispossessed by colonists because they are essentially “wicked” or “primitive”.[2] As Shylock knew to his cost, there is a long and poisonous tradition in Christian societies, rooted in verses like Matthew 27.25, of saying that the Jews deserve whatever suffering comes their way because of a whole litany of imaginary crimes.

Every attempt that has ever been made to connect a factual basis for differences in desert with differences in race, sex, or species has completely failed. That has not prevented such attempts from being believed, or from repeatedly leading to absolutely lamentable consequences—pogrom, genocide, factory farming, hunting to extinction, rape culture, and more. Nor, unfortunately, has it deterred people from continuing, even today, to look for such a factual basis in the pseudo-scientific endeavours of “race science” and “eugenics”. [3]

It is simply mistaken to think that any other species deserve to suffer either more, or less, than humans do—just as it is mistaken to think that there are any races that deserve to suffer, or that either sex deserves to suffer.

It is because all these endeavours are empty that I think desert makes no difference for animal rights, any more than it does for racial and sexual equality. If desert is (as I believe) a real notion in philosophical ethics, then strictly speaking, the original equality principleis wrong as it stands. It needed to be amended to the new principle which accommodates desert**.** But that is irrelevant for animal rights, because it is simply mistaken to think that any other species deserve to suffer either more, or less, than humans do—just as it is mistaken to think that there are any races that deserve to suffer, or that either sex deserves to suffer.

One way of bringing out vividly this equality of desert is to return to the question that I started with: “How should we think about the (other) animals?”

Principles like those outlined above, admirable though they of course are, have a marked tendency to make us think that ethics is basically just about acting rationally, in the sense that we never respond differently unless there is a difference in the situation

I believe that my own answer to that question marks an important shift: a shift, as we might call it, from a rationalist ethics to an ethics of love. Principles like those outlined above, admirable though they of course are, have a marked tendency to make us think that ethics is basically just about acting rationally, in the sense that we never respond differently unless there is a difference in the situation—where such differentiation is often taken to be the essence of what it is to be a good and rational agent. I don’t believe this; I believe we need more in our ethics than rationality as even-handed impartiality. In particular, the more that we need is love.

My animal ethics is, therefore, an ethics modelled after a famous injunction from Father Zossima in Dostoevsky’s The Brothers Karamazov

Love all God’s creation, the whole and every grain of sand in it. Love every leaf, every ray of God’s light. Love the animals, love the plants, love everything. If you love everything, you will perceive the divine mystery in things. Once you perceive it, you will begin to comprehend it better every day. And you will come at last to love the whole world with an all-embracing love.[4]

Father Zossima frames his ethics within his own, and Dostoevsky’s, Russian Orthodox Christianity. Outside that frame, atheists like Iris Murdoch can endorse essentially the same ethics. The call is to love everything, every part of the world and every creature in the world—as, at the deepest level, equally deserving.

[

SUGGESTED VIEWING In love with animals? With Peter Singer, Christopher Belshaw, Mary Ann Sieghart, Peter Egan, Myriam François](https://iai.tv/video/in-love-with-animals)

Now to love everything is, as Iris Murdoch famously insists, a matter of attention to it:[5] it is to love each thing as what it is. And a key part of what each thing is, is what kind of thing it is. And species are kinds of living things. So a key part of what each living thing is, is what species of thing it is.Where love for some animal is not just mushy sentimentality, but actually translates into particular action for its well-being, that means acting—within the holistic constraints imposed by the existence of all the other beings, and by the existence of the biosphere itself—for its specific kind of well-being. And what determines what well-being is for that animal specifically? Well, one key determinant, as the word “specifically” in fact suggests, is the animal’s species.

And so a proper understanding of animal rights is rooted not in the first position that I consider in this essay, anti-speciesism, but in the last position that I consider. Animal rights, so rooted, does not ignore differences of species; on the contrary, it begins from them. And animal rights, so rooted, is not simply about treating like cases alike. It is also about treating all cases with love.
